strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in AR image generation watermarking, which is understudied relative to diffusion models and practically relevant given recent deployments

Clear problem diagnosis with principled solution: identifies why naive token-level red-green watermarking fails (reconstruction mismatch, perturbation sensitivity) and proposes well-motivated cluster-based solution

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: ~4.75M images across multiple models (LlamaGen, RAR-XL), extensive perturbations (blur, noise, JPEG, S&P, color jitter), regeneration attacks, baselines, and thorough ablations
Strong empirical results with substantially improved robustness over post-hoc baselines, especially with cluster classifier (near-perfect TPR@FPR=1% on many perturbations)
Practical efficiency: verification runtime (10-25ms) competitive with DWT-DCT, far superior to diffusion in-generation methods requiring full inversion
Dual-approach design providing both training-free and learned variants for different deployment scenarios
Excellent reproducibility: extensive supplementary material with full results tables, visual examples, detailed experimental settings, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is applying k-means clustering to red-green watermarking (prior work Kirchenbauer et al.). Cluster classifier is standard VAE encoder + classification layer. Main innovation reduces to cluster-level vs token-level partitioning

Persistent critical robustness gaps: no robustness to geometric transforms (rotation, zoom); poor performance on blur (TPR 0.78-0.99 on Gaussian blur R3, Table 1) and salt-and-pepper noise; authors dismiss these as 'destructive' but watermarking should resist common manipulations

Methodological concerns: (1) prefix tuning over 8 candidates introduces selection bias and reproducibility issues; (2) binomial test assumes token independence which may be violated under perturbations; (3) only 2,000 images for ROC curves is modest; (4) detection threshold ρ not specified in main results

Concurrent work diminishes novelty: Wu et al. [33], Tong et al. [28], Jovanovic et al. [13] simultaneously propose similar approaches; IndexMark shows competitive/superior results in several settings (e.g., RAR-XL color jitter, regeneration); no clear advantage over concurrent methods established

Shallow cluster classifier analysis: no investigation of learned patterns, sensitivity to augmentation schedule, failure modes, or whether 100k training images suffice; unclear robustness if attacker uses different perturbations

Lack of theoretical justification: why k-means on codebook embeddings is optimal remains unanalyzed; no principled relationship between cluster quality and robustness; assumed connection between embedding distance and pixel-space similarity under perturbations not validated

Experimental design issues: (1) results heavily depend on prefix choice (Figure 5) via selection bias; (2) only AUC and TPR@FPR=1% reported, other operating points uninformative; (3) regeneration attacks averaged across methods; (4) vocabulary size effect (16k vs 1k) not discussed; (5) prefix selection procedure (Figure 3) not principled

Key practical gaps: prefix search requires ad-hoc tuning; no key management discussion; service provider must commit to prefix a priori; no analysis of false positive rates on unrelated images; no evaluation on non-class-conditional generation

Presentation issues: Table 1 extremely dense (better as separate per-model tables); Figure 3 variance across prefixes (critical issue) relegated to brief section 4.3; notation inconsistencies; Algorithm 1 could be more concise

strengths: Timely problem addressing watermarking for AR image models with growing practical importance
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 4.7M+ images, multiple models (LlamaGen, RAR), diverse perturbations, and detailed ablations
Clear problem formulation: identifies why naive red-green watermarking fails (token reconstruction errors) and proposes sensible solution
Strong empirical improvements: clustering dramatically outperforms token-level baseline, with Cluster Classifier providing additional gains
Fast verification runtime (10-25ms) comparable to lightweight post-hoc methods, significantly faster than diffusion-based watermarking
Good presentation quality with clear motivation, helpful visualizations, and extensive supplementary material with detailed results
Reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, extensive tables (7000+ results), promise to release code
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution (k-means clustering with uniform cluster coloring) is straightforward; the innovation is primarily in engineering application to AR models rather than fundamental algorithmic insight

Significant robustness gaps remain: destructive perturbations (salt-and-pepper noise achieves only 50-70% TPR@FPR=1%) and geometric transforms (acknowledged as unresolved limitation) severely limit practical applicability

Suspicious prefix tuning procedure: high variance across prefixes (shown in Figure 5); selecting best from 8 prefixes constitutes test-set hyperparameter optimization; unclear if results generalize to fixed prefixes, raising overfitting concerns
Noticeable quality-robustness tradeoff: FID increases from 4.50→4.85 (GPT-L, k=64) and 3.13→3.96 (RAR-XL); visual degradation apparent at k=8; tradeoff not thoroughly discussed

Unfair baseline comparisons: post-hoc methods (DWT-DCT, RivaGAN) not designed for in-generation settings; only one concurrent work (IndexMark) included despite multiple concurrent papers; conflates different problem formulations

Limited robustness analysis: no adaptive attacks assuming method knowledge; no token-swapping attacks; regeneration uses older models (SD1.5, SD2.1); no investigation of why certain prefixes work better for specific perturbations

High variance in results across prefixes (Tables 8-9) with substantial improvement from prefix selection, but unclear separation from clustering contribution; concerns about method generalization to new prefixes
Computational overhead under-discussed: 100k training images + ~12 hours GPU time for Cluster Classifier; requires empirical prefix search; overhead vs. verification speedup tradeoff not analyzed

Incomplete technical analysis: sensitivity to k-means initialization not discussed; assumption that similar tokens remain similar after perturbations not formally validated; learned cluster properties not visualized or analyzed

strengths: Addresses timely and important problem of watermarking emerging AR image models with clear technical motivation
Novel clustering-based approach is intuitive, well-motivated, and effectively improves robustness over naive token-level watermarking
Exceptional experimental rigor: 4.7M images generated, three models, extensive perturbations, comprehensive ablations, detailed documentation enabling reproducibility
Practical advantages over diffusion watermarking: fast verification (10-25ms), minimal FID impact at k=64, beats all baselines substantially
Two complementary approaches with clear trade-offs: training-free simplicity vs. finetuned robustness, giving practitioners options
Honest treatment of limitations; careful acknowledgment of what the method cannot handle (geometric transforms, specific settings)
Comprehensive supplementary material with full experimental details, algorithm descriptions, and sufficient information for reproduction
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: clustering-based solution is intuitive but relatively straightforward adaptation of existing red-green watermarking from LLMs to image domain
Concurrent works (Wu et al., Tong et al., Jovanovic et al.) pursue similar objectives, reducing novelty and exclusivity of contribution
Visible watermark meaningfully changes image appearance (Figure 1); perceptual impact not quantified, raising practical deployment concerns
Cannot handle geometric transforms (rotation, zoom) due to spatial misalignment—significant practical limitation left unresolved
Challenging perturbations remain problematic even with cluster classifier: salt-and-pepper and blur show moderate robustness degradation
Limited evaluation scope: only left-to-right generation order tested, only class-conditional generation (text-to-image not evaluated), only ImageNet domain
Hash prefix tuning approach is somewhat ad-hoc; significant variance in robustness across prefixes at low k (Figure 5) suggests the scheme may be sensitive to random seeds
Missing analysis: no quantification of token reconstruction accuracy with/without perturbations, no comparison of clustering to alternative methods, no adaptive attack evaluation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three AR models, eight+ perturbation types, geometric transformations, and regeneration attacks with ~5M generated images demonstrating systematic robustness analysis
Clear identification and resolution of why naive KGW watermarking fails on AR models (VQ-VAE quantization issues), with well-motivated clustering-based solution
Strong empirical results significantly outperforming existing baselines (DWT-DCT-SVD, RivaGAN, TrustMark, WMAR) across diverse perturbations while maintaining low FID degradation
Practical training-free base method immediately applicable to existing AR models without requiring modifications to generation process
Thorough ablation studies investigating key design choices (cluster count, green token fraction, penalty parameter, hash prefix tuning) with clear presentation via figures and tables
Good reproducibility support with detailed experimental setup, hyperparameter specifications, hardware configurations, and code release commitment
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: clustering for watermarking is established; contribution is primarily applying existing concepts to AR image generators rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques
Superficial security analysis in Section D without rigorous threat modeling, attack scenarios, or analysis of vulnerabilities if clustering scheme or prefix sets become known to adversaries
High sensitivity to hyperparameters (γ, δ, κ) with no principled method for setting values given security requirements; optimal parameters vary significantly across perturbation types
Classifier training uses unrealistic assumption of access to unwatermarked images as negative class, with limited analysis of generalization when watermarked images become the standard
Insufficient analysis of failure modes and edge cases; paper acknowledges some perturbations are 'hard to achieve' (strong blur, salt & pepper) but provides minimal investigation into why
Generalization concerns: only three related discrete token-based AR models tested; no evaluation on continuous latent space models or architectural variants, limiting claim generality
Hash prefix tuning (Section 3.4) is empirical and ad-hoc rather than principled; lacks theoretical justification for why this procedure yields robust prefixes
Missing computational analysis: no comparison of generation overhead, prefix tuning costs, or practical deployment implications versus other methods
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to 256×256 resolution; unclear how method scales to higher resolutions or how token distribution changes with model capacity
Statistical testing uses simple binomial test without discussion of detection threshold selection, calibration, or multiple comparison corrections

strengths: Addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: watermarking for autoregressive image models
Extensive experimental evaluation with comprehensive ablation studies across multiple perturbation types and models
Training-free baseline variant enables practical deployment without retraining generators
Honest reporting of limitations and parameter sensitivity with detailed experimental setup supporting reproducibility
Shows improved robustness against common image perturbations (Gaussian noise, JPEG compression, blur) compared to some baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: directly applies existing KGW token-level watermarking to AR models with clustering mechanism lacking rigorous justification for robustness gains
Substantial image quality degradation: FID increases of 50%+ (e.g., 6.51→10.00 for DWT-DCT-SVD), severely limiting practical applicability
Inconsistent improvements from clustering: non-clustering baseline often equals or outperforms clustering variants in Table 1, undermining the core contribution
High parameter sensitivity requiring careful tuning of multiple interdependent hyperparameters (k, δ, γ, hash prefix) with no clear selection guidance
Significant runtime overhead (5.75× verification slowdown) dismissed as negligible despite being objectively substantial for real-time deployment
Insufficient theoretical analysis: clustering benefit relies on intuition rather than formal justification or guarantees; no analysis of why perturbed images decode to semantically similar tokens
Limited security evaluation: no adversarial assessment of watermark removal attacks; prefix tuning potentially reduces effective key space

Evaluation gaps: only 2,000 images tested, limited to 2 AR architectures, complete watermark failures for certain perturbations (e.g., color jitter) unexplained, missing comparisons with other recent AR watermarking methods
Baseline inconsistencies: some existing methods (IndexMark, WMAR) achieve comparable performance; unclear if baselines are optimally tuned for AR models

Missing practical guidance: use cases for invisible watermarking poorly motivated; comparison to simpler alternatives (metadata, visible watermarks) absent; no clarity on when quality loss justifies robustness gains

strengths: Well-motivated clustering-based approach that cleverly improves robustness over token-level watermarking by operating at the discrete cluster level of AR codebooks
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation with ~5M generated images, multiple models, diverse realistic perturbations, geometric transformations, and systematic ablation studies

Strong empirical results demonstrating significantly improved robustness: cluster-based method achieves near-perfect detection (TPR≥0.99) under most perturbations while token-level baselines fail (Table 1)
Practical training-free design with negligible computational overhead (0.06s per image), enabling deployment without model retraining
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1), detailed algorithms, comprehensive appendix, and code availability commitment
Addresses an important and underexplored problem: watermarking for autoregressive image generators is critical for content authentication but had limited prior work
Systematic ablation studies (Section 4.3) thoroughly investigate effects of cluster count k, watermark strength δ, green token fraction γ, and hash prefix on performance and robustness
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: the fundamental idea of partitioning tokens and biasing generation is relatively straightforward; clustering for robustness is intuitive once the problem is framed. The work is primarily an engineering contribution

Shallow security analysis with no formal threat model: assumes codebook/encoder remain private (strong assumption), briefly dismisses hash prefix attacks without rigorous justification, lacks adversarial attack analysis, and provides no formal security guarantees

Insufficient theoretical understanding: no analysis of why clustering improves robustness beyond intuition; binomial hypothesis test is standard; missing formal analysis of detection probability vs. perturbation strength

Limited evaluation scope: only two AR model architectures (LLaMA-Gen variants, RAR-XL); 2,000 images for main evaluation is modest; sensitivity to ImageNet validation set for FID unexplored; false positive rates on unintended natural images not systematically studied

Incomplete hyperparameter guidance: Figure 4 shows detection failure/degradation under extreme perturbations; limited explanation of why certain perturbations are more destructive; no principled approach for selecting δ, γ, k across deployment scenarios; optimal hash prefix varies by perturbation type

Practical deployment questions unaddressed: unclear how end-users verify watermarks without clustering information; robustness to codebook access or reverse-engineering not analyzed; interaction of multiple watermarks not discussed; compatibility with model updates/variants not addressed

Baseline comparison limitations: most baselines not designed for AR generators; WMAR requires VAE fine-tuning making direct comparison unfair; limited comparison with other token-level AR watermarking methods; differences from concurrent work (Wu et al. [39]) not clearly delineated

Missing ablations and analysis: only k-means clustering explored; sensitivity to clustering algorithm unstudied; codebook robustness under model perturbations not analyzed; green/red set construction lacks formal justification; CLIP score degradation under certain perturbations not discussed
Generalization concerns: all experiments use ImageNet classes; evaluation on other datasets and text-to-image AR models missing; results on adversarially robust or specialized AR variants unavailable
